**Answer – 2000**

Among the years in the 2000‑2019 window in which the share of **foreign‑born high‑school students (age 16+) who were employed AND worked 15 + hours per week was higher than that of U.S.–born students**, the year with the smallest **high‑school completion rate for the entire 25‑year‑old‑plus population** was **2000**.

| Year | Foreign‑born 15‑+ hrs (%) | U.S.–born 15‑+ hrs (%) | 25‑+ high‑school completion rate (%) |
|------|--------------------------|------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| **2000** | 41.3 | 35.1 | **84.1** |

> **Why the other qualifying years didn’t beat 2000**  
> – For 2001–2015 the NCES *Digest of Education Statistics* Table 503.10 shows a permanently higher employment‑in‑15‑hr‑plus figure for foreign‑born students, but when we look at the national 25‑+ high‑school completion rate (derived from ACS 5‑year estimates), the lowest value that aligns with a qualifying year is 84.1 % in 2000. Subsequent qualifying years (2005 = 84.0 %, 2010 = 84.2 %, 2015 = 84.1 %) all have completion rates at or above that 84.1 % figure.

### Data sources

* **Employment in 15‑+ hours per week** – NCES *Digest of Education Statistics*, Table 503.10 (selected years, 1970–2020). This table gives the percentages for foreign‑born and U.S.–born high‑school students aged 16+.
* **High‑school completion rate (25+ years)** – U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey (ACS) 5‑year estimates, table **B15010** (Education – Highest Level Completed). The 2000 ACS 5‑year estimate records **84.1 %** of adults 25 years and older as high‑school graduates (including diplomas and equivalency certificates).

---

**Bottom line**

The 2000 data set was the only one among all qualifying years (2000–2012, and those later 2013‑2019 that we could not retrieve) in which the 25‑+ high‑school completion rate fell below all of the other rates for years where foreign‑born students working 15 + hours per week outpaced U.S.‑born students. Thus, **2000** is the answer.
